meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I am one of those who think like Nobel, that humanity will draw more good than evil from new discoveries'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Marie Curie: Pierre Curie ended his 6 June 1905 Nobel lecture with this thought. The popular wording matches neither standard English translation.

answer.label: Not Marie Curie — actually Pierre Curie
answer.authorDates: 1859–1906 · French physicist, 1903 Nobel laureate in Physics
answer.sourceLine: The thought is the closing sentence of Pierre Curie’s Nobel Lecture, “Radioactive Substances, Especially Radium,” given on 6 June 1905. The Nobel Foundation’s English text reads “I am one of those who believe with Nobel that mankind will derive more good than harm from the new discoveries.” The popular “think like Nobel… draw more good than evil” wording does not match either published English translation we checked.

source.heading: Where the line really comes from

docMeta.dd: 6 June 1905, for the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics
Nobel Lectures, Physics 1901–1921 (Elsevier, 1967); earlier rendering by Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg in Marie Curie’s Pierre Curie (Macmillan, 1923)

source.excerpt: It can even be thought that radium could become very dangerous in criminal hands, and here the question can be raised whether mankind benefits from knowing the secrets of Nature, whether it is ready to profit from it or whether this knowledge will not be harmful for it. The example of the discoveries of Nobel is characteristic, as powerful explosives have enabled man to do wonderful work. They are also a terrible means of destruction in the hands of great criminals who are leading the peoples towards war. I am one of those who believe with Nobel that mankind will derive more good than harm from the new discoveries.
trail: Wikiquote’s Marie Curie page lists the line under Misattributed and notes that it is the last sentence of her husband Pierre Curie’s Nobel lecture. Wikiquote: Marie Curie ↗

The Nobel Foundation’s text of Pierre Curie’s lecture, “Radioactive substances, especially radium” (Nobel Lecture, June 6, 1905), ends with “I am one of those who believe with Nobel that mankind will derive more good than harm from the new discoveries.” Nobel Lecture PDF ↗

Marie Curie’s own biography Pierre Curie (Macmillan, 1923, translated by Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg) opens with this passage as an epigraph, credited to “PIERRE CURIE, Nobel Conference, 1903”: “I am among those who believe with Nobel that humanity will obtain more good than evil from future discoveries.” Project Gutenberg #69617 ↗
The American Institute of Physics’ Curie exhibit quotes the same sentence and credits it to “Pierre Curie, Award Address for 1903 Nobel Prize for Physics.” AIP: Recognition and Disappointment ↗
source.excerptNote: This is the Nobel Foundation’s English text, from Nobel Lectures, Physics 1901–1921 (1967). The 1923 Kellogg translation ends “I am among those who believe with Nobel that humanity will obtain more good than evil from future discoveries.” The popular “think like Nobel, that humanity will draw more good than evil from new discoveries” matches neither.
source.rightsNote: The popular wording (“think like Nobel… draw more good than evil from new discoveries”) matches no published translation we could identify, so we assert no rights status for it. The 1923 Kellogg translation was published before 1931 and is public domain in the US. For the 1967 Elsevier text, NobelPrize.org ↗ states that “The Nobel Foundation’s copyright has expired.”

author.name: Pierre Curie
author.heading: About Pierre Curie
author.metaLine: 1859–1906 · French physicist, pioneer of radioactivity, 1903 Nobel laureate
author.bio: Pierre Curie was born in Paris on 15 May 1859. He shared one half of the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife, Marie Skłodowska-Curie, for their research on radioactivity; Henri Becquerel received the other half. Pierre gave the couple’s required Nobel lecture on 6 June 1905, and he was killed in a Paris street accident with a horse-drawn cart on 19 April 1906.

cite.sourceCitation: Pierre Curie, “Radioactive Substances, Especially Radium,” Nobel Lecture, June 6, 1905, in Nobel Lectures, Physics 1901–1921 (Amsterdam: Elsevier Publishing Company, 1967), p. 78. Earlier English rendering: Marie Curie, Pierre Curie, trans. Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg (New York: Macmillan, 1923), epigraph.

copyAttribution: "I am one of those who believe with Nobel that mankind will derive more good than harm from the new discoveries." — Pierre Curie (not Marie Curie), Nobel Lecture, "Radioactive Substances, Especially Radium," June 6, 1905. The popular "think like Nobel… draw more good than evil" wording is a loose rendering.

misattribution.heading: Why it gets pinned on Marie
misattribution.intro: Quote sites list this line under Marie Curie, usually in a loose wording that does not match any published translation. The sentence is her husband’s. Pierre spoke it at the end of the Nobel lecture the couple owed for their shared 1903 prize.

items.why: Quotepark lists the “think like Nobel” wording under Marie Curie, citing a 2007 medical-history book, but labels it Misattributed itself and points to Pierre’s lecture. Quotepark ↗. Wikiquote’s Marie Curie page also lists it as Misattributed. Wikiquote ↗

items.scope: A likely route to the confusion
items.why: In the English edition of Marie Curie’s biography of her husband, the passage is the opening epigraph, credited to “PIERRE CURIE, Nobel Conference, 1903.” A reader skimming a book with Marie Curie’s name on the cover could easily credit it to her. This is our inference, not a documented chain. Project Gutenberg ↗
The 1903 date belongs to the prize, which was awarded in December 1903. The lecture itself is dated June 6, 1905, after the Curies traveled to Stockholm. AIP ↗ · Nobel Lecture ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Pierre Curie said it, at the close of his Nobel Lecture of 6 June 1905: “I am one of those who believe with Nobel that mankind will derive more good than harm from the new discoveries.” NobelPrize.org ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Pierre Curie did not end his Nobel lecture on triumph. He ended on a warning. He had just described radium burns and said radium could become “very dangerous in criminal hands.” He then pointed to Alfred Nobel’s own explosives, which had “enabled man to do wonderful work” but were also “a terrible means of destruction in the hands of great criminals who are leading the peoples towards war.”
His closing sentence was a cautious bet on knowledge despite those risks. It was spoken in the city where Nobel’s prizes are awarded, and it named the man whose fortune paid for them.
context.detailsSummary: Three English versions of one sentence
detailsBody: 1923 (Kellogg translation): “I am among those who believe with Nobel that humanity will obtain more good than evil from future discoveries.” Gutenberg ↗
1967 (Nobel Lectures, Elsevier): “I am one of those who believe with Nobel that mankind will derive more good than harm from the new discoveries.” Nobel PDF ↗

Popular internet version: “I am one of those who think like Nobel, that humanity will draw more good than evil from new discoveries.” We found no published translation with this exact wording. Its translator and origin are unknown.
